title: The Companies Act, 2013
outcomes: Explain the meaning and features of a company and the corporate veil, including when courts lift it.
Classify companies by liability, members, control, access to capital and other special categories, and test whether a given company is a subsidiary, associate, small, Government or Section 8 company.
Describe promoters, formation and incorporation (Sections 3, 7, 9, 10) and compute the kinds of share capital.
Explain the memorandum and articles of association, the doctrine of ultra vires, constructive notice and indoor management, and apply them to problems.

meta.exam_tip: Problems on lifting the veil, ultra vires and indoor management are perennial; definitions of private company, OPC, small company, subsidiary/associate and Government company are asked as short notes or MCQ-style fact tests. Quote the section, then apply.

concepts.title: Company: meaning, applicability and features
body: The Companies Act, 2013 replaced the 1956 Act; it has 470 sections, seven schedules and 29 chapters, with much detail left to Rules. It applies to companies formed under it or earlier company laws, and to insurance, banking and electricity companies and companies under special Acts except where their own Acts conflict.
Section 2(20): a company is one incorporated under this Act or any previous company law. Jurists describe it as an artificial person created by law, with a separate entity and perpetual succession.

Features: separate legal entity, perpetual succession, limited liability, artificial legal person, and an optional common seal. Because the company owns its assets, even a near-100% shareholder cannot insure the company's goods in his own name (Macaura v. Northern Assurance Co., 1925).

blocks.title: Features of a company

concepts.analogy: A company is like a robot built by the law: it has its own name, bank account and property, but it needs humans (directors) to press its buttons.
concepts.work: Audit, tax and loan files are opened in the company's name, not the shareholders'. A CA must keep company and promoter transactions separate — mixing them is a classic audit finding.

concepts.title: Corporate veil theory and Salomon's case
body: The "corporate veil" is the legal curtain between the company and its members: the company's debts and wrongs are its own, and members are insulated from them.

Salomon v. Salomon & Co. Ltd. (House of Lords, 1897): Salomon sold his business to a company in which he held almost all the shares (his family held one share each) and took secured debentures. When the company failed, unsecured creditors argued it was just Salomon in disguise. Held: the company is a different person from its members, so Salomon, as a secured debenture-holder, ranked ahead of the unsecured creditors. This case is the foundation of separate corporate personality.
concepts.analogy: The veil is a glass partition in a bank: the customer (creditor) deals with the cashier (company), not with the people sitting behind.
concepts.work: When promoters lend to their own company, Salomon's principle is why their loans are genuine debts of the company — a CA must still check they are properly documented and approved.

concepts.title: Lifting (piercing) the corporate veil
body: Courts look behind the company at the real persons when the corporate form is misused, mainly where control rather than ownership is in question:

(1) Enemy character — to see whether a company is controlled by enemy aliens (Daimler Co. Ltd. v. Continental Tyre & Rubber Co.). (2) Protection of revenue — where a company is a sham to evade tax (Dinshaw Maneckjee Petit; Juggilal Kamlapat v. CIT). (3) Avoiding a legal obligation — a subsidiary created only to cut the bonus payable to workers was ignored (the Associated Rubber Industry case, Supreme Court). (4) Subsidiary acting as agent — parent and subsidiary treated as one unit (Merchandise Transport Ltd. v. British Transport Commission). (5) Fraud or improper purpose — a company formed to evade a former employee's non-compete covenant (Gilford Motor Co. v. Horne).
concepts.analogy: The veil is a mask. Courts let you wear it for ordinary business, but pull it off if you wear it to rob a bank.
concepts.work: In tax scrutiny, insolvency and fraud investigations, authorities lift the veil to reach promoters. CAs advising on group structures must ensure each entity has a real business purpose.

concepts.title: Classes of companies — by liability
body: Company limited by shares (Section 2(22)): under the memorandum a member can be asked to pay only what remains unpaid on his shares; that amount can be called at any time during the company's life or in winding up.

Company limited by guarantee (Section 2(21)): members undertake in the memorandum to contribute a fixed amount to the assets if the company is wound up; payable only then. Such companies suit bodies funded by fees, donations or endowments. Its membership can carry special privileges, so its right to refuse a transfer stands on a different footing (Narendra Kumar Agarwal v. Saroj Maloo).
Unlimited company (Section 2(92)): no limit on members' liability; each member can be called upon (through the liquidator) for the whole deficiency, with a right of contribution from the others.

blocks.title: How far can a member be made to pay?

concepts.analogy: Shares: you owe the rest of the ticket price. Guarantee: you promised a fixed donation if the club closes. Unlimited: you signed a blank cheque.
concepts.work: Before advising a client to subscribe to partly paid shares, a CA explains that the unpaid amount is a real future liability.

concepts.title: Classes by members: OPC, private, small and public companies
body: One Person Company (Section 2(62); Section 3(1)(c)): a private company with only one member. The memorandum names a nominee who becomes member on the subscriber's death or incapacity; the nominee's written consent is filed at incorporation and the member may change the nominee by notice (this does not count as altering the memorandum). Eligibility is confined to individuals holding Indian citizenship — resident (stayed at least 120 days in India in the preceding financial year) or not — may form one or be a nominee; no person may form more than one OPC or be nominee in more than one; a minor cannot be member or nominee; an OPC cannot be a Section 8 company or carry on non-banking financial investment activity. The sole member may also be the director.

Private company (Section 2(68)): its articles (i) restrict transfer of shares, (ii) limit members to 200 (except an OPC) — joint holders count as one, and present and former employee-members are excluded — and (iii) prohibit invitations to the public to subscribe for its securities. Minimum 2 members; no minimum paid-up capital now.

Small company (Section 2(85)): a company other than a public company whose paid-up capital does not exceed ₹10 crore and whose turnover in the preceding year does not exceed ₹100 crore (limits as given in the study material for this attempt); a holding or subsidiary company, a Section 8 company and a company under a special Act cannot be a small company.

Public company (Section 2(71)): one that is not a private company; minimum 7 members, no maximum. A private company that is a subsidiary of a public company is deemed public, even if its articles say private.

blocks.title: Classes of companies

concepts.analogy: An OPC is a single-seat car, a private company a family car with a 200-seat cap and locked doors, a public company a bus anyone can board.
concepts.work: Classification decides compliance: small companies and OPCs get lighter rules (e.g. fewer board meetings, no cash-flow statement for OPCs and small companies). A CA tests the definitions every year because turnover and holding status change.

concepts.title: Classes by control and access to capital
body: Holding company (Section 2(46)) and subsidiary (Section 2(87)): A is a subsidiary of B if B either (i) decides who sits on A's Board — meaning B, at its own discretion, can put in or remove most or all of A's directors — or (ii) commands over 50% of A's total votes, by itself or counting the votes of B's own subsidiaries. Control through another subsidiary counts; "company" includes any body corporate; prescribed classes may not have layers of subsidiaries beyond the prescribed number.

Associate company (Section 2(6)): a company that another company can significantly influence — by holding 20% or more of the total votes, or by sharing in or controlling its business decisions through an agreement — without it being a subsidiary; it includes a joint venture company.
Listed company (Section 2(52)): any of its securities is listed on a recognised stock exchange (prescribed classes excepted). Unlisted: all others.

blocks.title: Group structure of Helix Ltd

concepts.analogy: Holding over 50% of votes is holding the steering wheel; 20% is sitting in the front seat giving directions.
concepts.work: Consolidated financial statements, related-party disclosures and audit-rotation rules all depend on these tests. Group auditors map every entity's voting power and board-appointment rights.

concepts.title: Other classes: Government, foreign, Section 8, dormant, Nidhi, PFI
body: Government company (Section 2(45)): at least 51% of paid-up share capital (total voting power where differential-voting shares exist) held by the Central Government, one or more State Governments, or both together; includes a subsidiary of a Government company. Its name must end with "Limited".

Foreign company (Section 2(42)): incorporated outside India and having a place of business in India (itself, through an agent, physically or electronically) and conducting any business activity in India.

Section 8 company: set up for objects such as trade promotion, arts, science, sport, education, research, social welfare, religion, charity or the environment; applies profits to its objects and pays no dividend; registered under a licence (power delegated to the Registrar) without "Limited"/"Private Limited" in its name (names like Foundation, Forum, Association, Council). The licence may be revoked after notice and hearing for breach of conditions, fraud or public-interest reasons; the company may then be wound up or amalgamated with a similar one. Default: fine ₹10 lakh to ₹1 crore on the company and ₹25,000 to ₹25 lakh on officers in default (fraud — Section 447). It may call a general meeting on 14 clear days' notice; a partnership firm may be its member.

Dormant company (Section 455): a company set up to hold an asset or IP or for a project yet to start, which has had no significant accounting transaction, or an inactive company (no business, no significant accounting transaction, or no filing of financial statements and annual returns, for the last two financial years) — may apply to the Registrar for dormant status. Paying ROC fees, statutory payments, allotting shares to meet legal requirements and office upkeep are not significant transactions.

Nidhi (Section 406): notified by the Central Government as a Nidhi or Mutual Benefit Society, to promote thrift and saving among members. Public Financial Institution (Section 2(72)): LIC, IDFC, the specified UTI company, institutions notified under the old Section 4A, and others notified in consultation with RBI if set up under a Central/State Act or at least 51% Government-held.
concepts.analogy: These are special-purpose vehicles in the company "garage": an ambulance (Section 8), a parked car (dormant), a government jeep (Government company).
concepts.work: Section 8 companies are a common NGO structure; their auditors check that no dividend or disguised distribution reaches members and that licence conditions are met.

concepts.title: Promoters, formation and incorporation (Sections 2(69), 3, 7, 9, 10)
body: Promoter (Section 2(69)): a person named as such in a prospectus or identified in the annual return; or who controls the company's affairs directly or indirectly; or on whose advice the Board is accustomed to act. Professionals acting only in a professional capacity are not promoters.
Section 3: a public company may be formed by 7 or more persons, a private company by 2 or more, and an OPC by 1, for any lawful purpose, by subscribing to the memorandum and registering.

Section 7: file with the Registrar (where the registered office will be) — memorandum and articles signed by subscribers; a declaration by a professional engaged in formation (advocate, CA, cost accountant or CS in practice) and by a director/manager/secretary named in the articles that all requirements are met; declarations by subscribers and first directors about no conviction or fraud in the last five years and correctness of documents; correspondence address; particulars and identity proof of subscribers; and particulars, DIN, interests and consent of first directors. The Registrar issues a certificate of incorporation and a Corporate Identity Number (CIN). Copies must be kept at the registered office till dissolution. False information — fraud under Section 447 for the persons concerned; if incorporation itself was obtained by fraud, the Tribunal may regulate management, make members' liability unlimited, strike off the name, order winding up, or pass other orders, after hearing the company. Filing is done through SPICe (Simplified Proforma for Incorporating Company Electronically).

Section 9: from the date in the certificate, the subscribers and later members form a body corporate with perpetual succession and power to hold property, contract, and sue and be sued. Section 10: the memorandum and articles bind the company and members as if signed by each, and money payable by a member under them is a debt due to the company.
concepts.analogy: Incorporation is the company's birth certificate: the CIN is its Aadhaar number, and from that date it lives as a separate person.
concepts.work: A practising CA can certify the Section 7 declaration and is often the professional who files SPICe forms. A false declaration exposes the CA to fraud proceedings — due diligence on subscribers is essential.

concepts.title: Capital and shares (Sections 2(8), 2(50), 2(86), 2(15), 2(84), 43, 44, 45)
body: Capital means share capital. A share is not a sum of money but an interest in the company measured by money, made up of rights under the memorandum, articles and the Act (Borland's Trustee v. Steel Bros.). Shareholders are not part-owners of the company's undertaking.

Section 2(84): "share" means a share in the share capital and includes stock. Section 44: shares are movable property, transferable as the articles provide. Section 45: each share carries a distinctive number, except shares held in a depository in dematerialised form.

Section 43: share capital of a company limited by shares is of two kinds — equity (with voting rights, or with differential rights as to dividend, voting or otherwise under the rules) and preference (carrying a preferential right to dividend at a fixed amount or rate, and to repayment of capital on winding up). A private company may exclude Section 43 through its memorandum or articles.

Section 60: where a company states its authorised capital in a notice, advertisement, letter or bill-head, it must state the subscribed and paid-up capital equally prominently; default — penalty ₹10,000 on the company and ₹5,000 on each officer in default.

blocks.title: Kinds of share capital

concepts.analogy: Authorised capital is the size of the cake you are allowed to bake; issued is what you put on the table; subscribed is what guests take; called-up is what you ask them to pay for now; paid-up is what they have actually paid.
concepts.work: Every balance sheet under Schedule III shows authorised, issued, subscribed and paid-up capital. Auditors reconcile these with the memorandum, ROC filings and the register of members.

concepts.title: Memorandum of Association (Section 4)
body: The memorandum is the company's charter: it fixes the objects and the limits of its powers, so shareholders and outsiders know what the company may do. It is a public document (Section 399).

Clauses: (a) Name — ending with "Limited" (public) or "Private Limited" (private); not required for Section 8 companies; OPCs show "One Person Company" below the name; Government companies end with "Limited". (b) Registered office — the State. (c) Objects — and matters necessary in furtherance; if activities change, the name must be brought in line within six months. (d) Liability — limited by shares (unpaid amount) or by guarantee (amount each member will contribute on winding up while a member or within a year after ceasing, including winding-up costs), or unlimited. (e) Capital — authorised capital divided into shares of fixed amount, and the shares each subscriber takes (at least one). (f) Association/subscription clause — subscribers' details; for an OPC, the nominee.

Forms: Tables A to E of Schedule I (A — limited by shares; B — guarantee without share capital; C — guarantee with share capital; D — unlimited; E — unlimited with share capital). Subscribers sign in the presence of a witness; a company can subscribe through an agent; a minor cannot (a guardian subscribing for him is treated as subscribing personally). Anything in the memorandum contrary to the Act has no effect.
concepts.analogy: The memorandum is the boundary wall of the company's plot: everything the company does must stay inside it.
concepts.work: Before a client starts a new line of business, a CA checks the objects clause; if needed, the clause is altered by special resolution and filed with the ROC before the new activity begins.

concepts.title: Doctrine of ultra vires
body: Ultra vires means "beyond the powers". An act or contract outside the objects in the memorandum (or the Act) is ultra vires the company and wholly void: the company cannot sue or be sued on it, and it cannot be ratified even by all the shareholders, nor validated by estoppel, acquiescence or delay.

Ashbury Railway Carriage & Iron Co. Ltd. v. Riche (1875): a company formed to make railway carriages and act as mechanical engineers and general contractors agreed to finance construction of a railway in Belgium; shareholders even ratified it. Held: void — "general contractors" had to be read with the main objects.

Distinguish: ultra vires the directors but within the company's powers — members can ratify by resolution in general meeting; ultra vires the articles but within the memorandum — regularised by altering the articles by special resolution; within powers but done irregularly — members can validate.

Effect on outsiders: a lender to an ultra vires purpose cannot recover as a debt, but may obtain an injunction to stop the company spending money still unspent and recover it in specie; if the money paid off lawful debts of the company, he is subrogated to those creditors to that extent. Since objects can now be altered by special resolution, the doctrine has lost much of its sting.
concepts.analogy: If a cricket bat company signs a contract to run an airline, the umpire (court) declares "no ball" — and no amount of team agreement makes it a legal ball.
concepts.work: Bankers and auditors check that a large contract or loan falls within the objects; an ultra vires guarantee or investment cannot be enforced and must be flagged.

concepts.title: Articles of Association (Section 5)
body: The articles are the internal rules for managing the company — subordinate to the memorandum and the Act (Ashbury v. Riche). They create rights and obligations between the company and its members.

Section 5: the articles contain the regulations for management and prescribed matters (plus anything else the company needs). They may contain entrenchment provisions — specified articles can be altered only under conditions stricter than a special resolution; entrenchment may be made at formation or later by all members (private company) or by special resolution (public company), and the Registrar must be notified. Forms: Tables F to J of Schedule I; a company may adopt the model articles in whole or part, and model articles apply to the extent its registered articles do not exclude or modify them. Articles are altered by special resolution.

blocks.title: Memorandum vs Articles

concepts.analogy: If the memorandum is the constitution, the articles are the house rules of the parliament that runs under it.
concepts.work: Auditors read the articles for borrowing limits, quorum, signing authority and share-transfer restrictions before testing compliance.

concepts.title: Constructive notice and the doctrine of indoor management
body: Constructive notice: registered documents (memorandum, articles, registrable special resolutions) are public — anyone may inspect them electronically under Section 399 on paying the fee. So every person dealing with the company is presumed to know and understand their contents, whether or not he has read them; he cannot claim rights under a contract beyond the company's powers or the directors' authority as stated there.

Indoor management (Royal British Bank v. Turquand): an outsider need not inquire into the company's internal proceedings. If an act is permitted by the memorandum and articles subject to an internal formality (e.g. a resolution that is not registrable), he may assume the formality has been complied with. In Turquand, directors could borrow only as authorised by a general-meeting resolution; the bank could assume the resolution existed, and the bond was enforceable.

Exceptions — no protection where: (a) the outsider had actual or constructive knowledge of the irregularity (Howard v. Patent Ivory Manufacturing Co.; Morris v. Kanssen — insiders such as directors cannot rely on it); (b) the circumstances were suspicious or the transaction unusual, so he should have inquired (Anand Bihari Lal v. Dinshaw & Co. — property transferred by an accountant without authority; Haughton & Co. v. Nothard, Lowe & Wills Ltd.); (c) forgery — a forged document is a nullity (Ruben v. Great Fingall Consolidated).
concepts.analogy: You must read the notice on the shop door (constructive notice), but you need not check the shop's back-office files (indoor management) — unless something looks fishy, you are an insider, or the signature is forged.
concepts.work: Lenders obtain certified board resolutions and verify signatories exactly because the indoor-management rule will not protect them if the transaction is unusual or the documents forged.

illustrations.title: Five kinds of capital from one set of facts
illustrations.q: Nirmal Textiles Ltd has an authorised capital of 10,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each. It offered 6,00,000 shares to the public, of which 5,50,000 were applied for and allotted. It has called ₹8 per share. Holders of 20,000 shares have not paid the last call of ₹3 per share. Compute the authorised, issued, subscribed, called-up and paid-up capital, and the uncalled amount.

given.text: Authorised 10,00,000 shares × ₹10; issued 6,00,000; subscribed 5,50,000; called ₹8; calls in arrears 20,000 × ₹3.

solution.title: Uncalled capital and unissued capital
solution.text: Uncalled = 5,50,000 × (₹10 − ₹8) = ₹11,00,000 — this is the members' remaining liability. Unissued authorised capital = ₹1,00,00,000 − ₹60,00,000 = ₹40,00,000.

checks.label: paid-up capital = called-up − calls in arrears

illustrations.title: Extent of a member's liability in three companies
illustrations.q: Meera is a member of (a) Alpha Ltd, holding 2,000 shares of ₹10, ₹6 paid; (b) Beta Foundation, a company limited by guarantee without share capital, in whose memorandum she undertook ₹25,000; and (c) Gamma Unlimited Company. All three go into liquidation with heavy deficits. How much more can Meera be asked to pay in each?

solution.provision: Section 2(22): in a company limited by shares, liability is limited to the amount unpaid on the shares. Section 2(21): in a guarantee company, liability is the amount undertaken in the memorandum, payable on winding up. Section 2(92): an unlimited company has no limit on members' liability.
solution.facts: Alpha: 2,000 shares with ₹4 unpaid each. Beta: undertaking ₹25,000. Gamma: unlimited.
solution.analysis: Alpha: 2,000 × ₹4 = ₹8,000. Beta: ₹25,000, enforceable only because Beta is being wound up. Gamma: the liquidator may call on her for the whole deficiency, subject to her right of contribution from other members.
solution.conclusion: Maximum further payment: Alpha ₹8,000; Beta ₹25,000; Gamma — no limit.

illustrations.title: Mapping a group: subsidiary or associate?
illustrations.q: Helix Ltd holds 60% of the voting power of Ash Ltd and 30% of Cedar Ltd; Ash Ltd holds 55% of Birch Ltd and 25% of Cedar Ltd. Helix holds 25% of Deodar Ltd, and 15% of Elm Ltd but has the right under Elm's articles to appoint 4 of its 7 directors. Determine the status of each company in relation to Helix.

solution.text: Tests: Section 2(87) — subsidiary if the holding company controls Board composition or more than one-half of total voting power, on its own or together with its subsidiaries; control exercised through a subsidiary counts. Section 2(6) — associate if at least 20% voting power (significant influence) but not a subsidiary.

illustrations.title: An ultra vires loan
illustrations.q: The objects clause of Sona Biscuits Ltd covers only manufacture and sale of bakery products. Its directors borrow ₹50 lakh from Vimal Finance to set up a film-production unit, and the shareholders unanimously approve. The venture fails. ₹12 lakh of the loan remains unspent in a separate account, and ₹10 lakh was used to pay the company's flour suppliers. Vimal sues for ₹50 lakh. Advise.

solution.provision: Doctrine of ultra vires (Ashbury Railway Carriage & Iron Co. v. Riche): a contract beyond the objects in the memorandum is void and cannot be ratified even unanimously. Every person dealing with the company has constructive notice of the memorandum. A lender may, however, restrain the company by injunction from parting with unspent money and recover it, and to the extent the money discharged lawful debts of the company he can recover that amount by stepping into those creditors' shoes.
solution.facts: Film production is outside the objects. The loan of ₹50 lakh was for that purpose; ₹12 lakh is unspent; ₹10 lakh paid lawful debts (flour suppliers).
solution.analysis: The loan contract is ultra vires and void; the unanimous approval does not cure it. Vimal cannot sue on the contract for ₹50 lakh. But the unspent ₹12 lakh still belongs to Vimal and can be followed by injunction, and ₹10 lakh applied to lawful debts can be recovered by subrogation.
solution.conclusion: Vimal cannot recover ₹50 lakh as a debt. It may recover ₹12 lakh (unspent) and ₹10 lakh (used for lawful debts) — ₹22 lakh in all — and loses the rest.

illustrations.title: Indoor management — and a forged certificate
illustrations.q: (a) The articles of Kiran Steel Ltd allow directors to borrow beyond ₹1 crore only with an ordinary resolution of members. Two directors borrow ₹1.5 crore from a bank without such a resolution. (b) The company secretary of the same company issues a share certificate to Lalit bearing the company seal and the forged signatures of two directors. Can the bank and Lalit hold the company bound?

solution.provision: Doctrine of indoor management (Royal British Bank v. Turquand): an outsider may assume that internal formalities required by the articles have been complied with. It does not apply where the outsider knew of the irregularity, where the circumstances should have raised suspicion, or in a case of forgery, which is a nullity (Ruben v. Great Fingall Consolidated).
solution.facts: (a) The power to borrow exists in the articles subject to an internal ordinary resolution, which is not a registrable document. (b) The share certificate carried forged signatures.
solution.analysis: (a) The bank had constructive notice of the articles but not of whether the internal resolution was passed; it was entitled to assume it. (b) Forgery is outside the rule; a forged certificate is a nullity and cannot bind the company.
solution.conclusion: (a) The company is bound to repay the bank. (b) Lalit cannot hold the company bound by the forged certificate (his remedy is against the wrongdoer).

jobs.title: Incorporating a client's start-up
jobs.role: CA in practice filing SPICe forms
jobs.situation: Two friends want to start a software company with ₹1 lakh capital; one is a non-resident Indian citizen.
steps: Advise a private company (2 members minimum) — or an OPC if only one would be a member (the NRI citizen could form an OPC since non-residents who are Indian citizens are eligible).
Draft the memorandum (name ending "Private Limited", State, objects covering software and allied services, liability, capital) and articles restricting share transfer.
Collect subscribers' and directors' declarations, identity proofs, DIN and consents; give your own professional declaration only after verifying them.
File through SPICe; after the certificate of incorporation and CIN, keep copies at the registered office.
jobs.takeaway: Your professional declaration under Section 7 is a legal statement — false information is treated as fraud under Section 447.
jobs.think: Why must the objects clause be drafted wide enough?
jobs.answer: Acts outside the objects are ultra vires and void; a narrow objects clause would force an alteration before entering any new line of business.

jobs.title: Is our client a small company this year?
jobs.situation: A private company has paid-up capital of ₹6 crore and last year's turnover of ₹92 crore. It has just acquired 70% of another company.
steps: Apply Section 2(85) limits (paid-up up to ₹10 crore, turnover up to ₹100 crore) — both are met.
Check exclusions: by acquiring 70% it has become a holding company, so it is NOT a small company.
Update the audit plan: small-company exemptions (e.g. cash-flow statement relief) no longer apply; consolidation is now required.
jobs.takeaway: Meeting the money limits is not enough — holding/subsidiary status takes a company out of the small-company class.

jobs.title: Verifying authority before disbursing a loan
jobs.role: CA in a bank's credit team
jobs.situation: A company's CFO submits a loan application signed by one director, with a board resolution copy.
steps: Check the memorandum (borrowing within objects/powers) and articles (who can sign, borrowing limits) — you have constructive notice of them.
Rely on indoor management for internal steps, but not where anything is unusual — e.g. an amount far above past borrowing or signed by an unexpected person.
Verify signatures independently; the rule offers no protection against forgery.
jobs.takeaway: Read the public documents; assume internal regularity only when nothing looks odd.

mcqs.q: Which case laid the foundation of the principle that a company is a legal person distinct from its members?
options: Ashbury Railway Carriage Co. v. Riche
Daimler Co. v. Continental Tyre Co.
mcqs.explain: Salomon's case (House of Lords, 1897).

mcqs.q: A shareholder holding nearly all the shares insured the company's timber in his own name. After a fire, the insurer was:
options: Not liable — he had no insurable interest in company property
Liable, as he was the real owner
mcqs.explain: Macaura v. Northern Assurance Co. (1925).

mcqs.q: The veil was lifted in Gilford Motor Co. v. Horne because the company was formed:
options: To evade a contractual non-compete obligation
mcqs.explain: Fraud/improper purpose — formed to get round Horne's covenant.

mcqs.q: Maximum number of members of a private company (excluding present and past employee-members) is:
mcqs.explain: Section 2(68)(ii).

mcqs.q: Which is NOT a requirement in the articles of a private company under Section 2(68)?
options: Prohibition of invitation to the public to subscribe
mcqs.explain: The minimum paid-up capital requirement has been removed.

mcqs.q: For an Indian citizen to be "resident in India" for forming an OPC, he must have stayed in India in the preceding financial year for at least:
mcqs.explain: Per the OPC eligibility rule as given in the study material (non-residents who are Indian citizens are also eligible).

mcqs.q: P Ltd holds 35% of the voting power of Q Ltd, and P's subsidiary R Ltd holds 20% of Q Ltd. Q Ltd is:
options: An associate of P Ltd only
A holding company of P Ltd
mcqs.explain: 35% + 20% = 55%, more than one-half, controlled together with a subsidiary — Section 2(87).

mcqs.q: Significant influence for an associate company means control of at least ____ of total voting power:
mcqs.explain: Section 2(6) explanation; or control of/participation in business decisions under an agreement.

mcqs.q: Central Government holds 30% and two State Governments together hold 22% of the paid-up capital of X Ltd. X Ltd is:
options: Not a Government company — no single Government holds 51%
mcqs.explain: 30% + 22% = 52%; holdings of Central and State Governments are combined — Section 2(45).

mcqs.q: A Section 8 company may call its general meeting by giving clear notice of:
mcqs.explain: Exemption for Section 8 companies — 14 days instead of 21.

mcqs.q: A public company may be formed by a minimum of:
mcqs.explain: Section 3(1)(a).

mcqs.q: Shares of ₹10 each, ₹8 called; 50,000 shares subscribed; calls in arrears ₹40,000. Paid-up capital is:
Under Section 43, preference share capital carries a preferential right as to:
options: Dividend and repayment of capital on winding up
mcqs.explain: Both preferences are essential to preference shares.

mcqs.q: An act ultra vires the memorandum:
options: Is void and cannot be ratified even by all the shareholders
Can be ratified by a special resolution
Can be ratified by the Board
mcqs.explain: Ashbury Railway Carriage Co. v. Riche.

mcqs.q: The doctrine of indoor management protects an outsider EXCEPT where:
options: The document relied on is a forgery
A non-registrable resolution was not passed
An internal formality was skipped by the directors
The outsider did not inspect the minutes book
mcqs.explain: Ruben v. Great Fingall Consolidated — forgery is a nullity.

mcqs.q: The forms of memorandum of association are given in which Tables of Schedule I?
mcqs.explain: Articles are in Tables F to J.

mcqs.q: Which company can be a "small company"?
options: A private company with paid-up capital ₹8 crore and turnover ₹90 crore, not a holding or subsidiary
A public company with paid-up capital ₹2 crore
A private company with turnover ₹150 crore
A Section 8 company with turnover ₹5 crore
mcqs.explain: Section 2(85): other than public company; paid-up ≤ ₹10 crore and turnover ≤ ₹100 crore; Section 8 and holding/subsidiary excluded.

questions.q: Ravi sold his trading business to a buyer and agreed not to compete within the same city for three years. Six months later Ravi formed Rapid Traders Pvt Ltd, held 98% of its shares himself (his wife holding 2%), and began the same trade in the same city through the company. The buyer seeks to restrain the company. Ravi argues the company is a separate person. Decide.

model.provision: A company is a legal person distinct from its members (Salomon v. Salomon & Co. Ltd.). Yet courts will look behind that separate personality when the company is a mere tool for fraud or for dodging a legal duty (Gilford Motor Co. v. Horne).
model.facts: Ravi was bound by a non-compete covenant. He formed a company he wholly controls and carried on the prohibited trade through it.
model.analysis: The company is a mere cloak to evade Ravi's personal obligation. Its separate personality is being used for an improper purpose, which is a recognised ground for lifting the veil.
model.conclusion: The court will disregard the separate entity and restrain both Ravi and the company from carrying on the business.

scheme.pt: Lifting the veil for fraud/evasion — Gilford Motor
Application: company formed to evade covenant
Conclusion: injunction against Ravi and company

remarks: Start with the rule (separate entity) before the exception — examiners award a mark for each.
mistakes: Concluding that the company cannot be restrained because it is a separate person.
tips: Name the ground: "company formed for fraud / to evade a legal obligation".

questions.q: What is a One Person Company? State any six significant points relating to its formation and restrictions.

model.text: Section 2(62): a One Person Company is a company with only one person as member; under Section 3(1)(c) it is formed as a private company.

items: Only a natural person who is an Indian citizen, resident in India or not, may incorporate an OPC or be its nominee.
The memorandum names a nominee who becomes the member on the subscriber's death or incapacity; the nominee's prior written consent is filed with the incorporation documents.
The member may change the nominee by notice to the company; this is not an alteration of the memorandum.
No person may incorporate more than one OPC or be a nominee in more than one.
A minor cannot be a member or nominee or hold shares with beneficial interest.
It cannot be incorporated as, or converted into, a Section 8 company, and cannot carry on non-banking financial investment activities.
No minimum paid-up capital is prescribed; the sole member can also be the director; "One Person Company" is written below its name.

remarks: Nominee rules and the one-OPC limit are the most expected points.
mistakes: Saying a foreign national or a company can form an OPC.
Saying an OPC can be a public company.
tips: Number the points; one line each.

questions.q: Explain the contents (clauses) of the Memorandum of Association of a company limited by shares under Section 4 of the Companies Act, 2013.

items: Name clause — ending with "Limited" or "Private Limited" (not needed for Section 8 companies); "One Person Company" below an OPC's name.
Registered office clause — the State in which the registered office will be situated.
Objects clause — the objects for which the company is incorporated and matters necessary in furtherance; if activities change, the name must be changed within six months to match.
Liability clause — that members' liability is limited to the amount unpaid on their shares.
Capital clause — authorised capital divided into shares of a fixed amount, and the number of shares each subscriber agrees to take (not less than one).
Association/subscription clause — details of subscribers who wish to form the company; for an OPC, the name of the nominee.

model.text: The memorandum follows Table A of Schedule I, is signed by the subscribers before a witness, and anything in it contrary to the Act is void.

remarks: Give one line of meaning for each clause, not just its name.
mistakes: Mixing in articles matters such as quorum or board meetings.
tips: Hook: "N-R-O-L-C-S" — Name, Registered office, Objects, Liability, Capital, Subscription.

questions.q: The articles of Pearl Foods Ltd require two directors to sign any cheque above ₹10 lakh. The accounts manager of the company, holding no power of attorney, sells the company's warehouse to Mr. Joshi and receives the price. Mr. Joshi claims protection under the doctrine of indoor management. Decide.

model.provision: Doctrine of indoor management (Royal British Bank v. Turquand): outsiders may presume internal regularity. Exception: it does not protect a person where the circumstances are suspicious or the act is apparently outside the authority of the officer — he must inquire (Anand Bihari Lal v. Dinshaw & Co.).
model.facts: An accounts manager, without any power of attorney, purported to sell the company's immovable property to Mr. Joshi.
model.analysis: Selling a warehouse is plainly outside the normal authority of an accounts manager. The transaction should have put Mr. Joshi on inquiry; having made none, he cannot presume that the company authorised it.
model.conclusion: The doctrine does not protect Mr. Joshi; the transfer is void as against the company.

scheme.pt: Application to accounts manager selling property

remarks: Candidates who explain the rule and then the specific exception score full marks.
mistakes: Applying the rule blindly in favour of Mr. Joshi.
tips: Cite Anand Bihari Lal v. Dinshaw & Co. if you remember it; the reasoning matters more.

questions.q: Udaan Motors Ltd has authorised capital of 5,00,000 shares of ₹100 each. It issued 3,00,000 shares, of which 2,80,000 were subscribed. ₹70 per share has been called. Calls of ₹20 per share on 5,000 shares are unpaid. Compute the authorised, issued, subscribed, called-up and paid-up capital, citing the definitions.

model.text: Definitions: authorised — Section 2(8); issued — 2(50); subscribed — 2(86); called-up — 2(15); paid-up = called-up less calls in arrears — 2(64).

remarks: Paid-up must deduct calls in arrears.
mistakes: Computing called-up on issued rather than subscribed shares.
tips: Work top-down: authorised → issued → subscribed → called-up → paid-up.

questions.q: Distinguish between the Memorandum of Association and the Articles of Association on any four bases.

head: Basis
Memorandum of Association
Articles of Association
rows: Defines objects and powers; relationship with outsiders
Defines how objects are pursued; relationship between company and members
Only in the manner and cases the Act allows; often needs approval of the Regional Director, Central Government or Tribunal
By special resolution, subject to the Act and the memorandum
Ultra vires the memorandum — void, cannot be ratified even unanimously
Ultra vires the articles but within the memorandum — can be ratified by altering the articles by special resolution
Tables A to E, Schedule I
Tables F to J, Schedule I
model.title: Memorandum vs Articles

remarks: Alteration and ultra vires are the bases examiners look for first.
mistakes: Saying the memorandum can never be altered.

summary: Section 2(20) company; features — separate entity (Salomon; Macaura), perpetual succession, limited liability, artificial person, optional seal.
Veil lifted for: enemy character (Daimler), tax evasion (Dinshaw Maneckjee Petit), avoiding obligations (Associated Rubber), agency (Merchandise Transport), fraud (Gilford Motor).

Classes: shares/guarantee/unlimited; OPC/private (≤200)/public (≥7); holding-subsidiary (Board or >50% votes)/associate (≥20%); listed; Government (≥51%); foreign; Section 8; dormant; Nidhi; PFI; small (≤₹10 cr capital, ≤₹100 cr turnover, not holding/subsidiary/Section 8).
Formation: 7/2/1 persons (Section 3); incorporation documents, certificate and CIN (Section 7); effect (Section 9); MoA/AoA bind as contract (Section 10).
Capital: authorised → issued → subscribed → called-up → paid-up. Shares: movable property; equity (incl. DVR) and preference.

MoA: name, registered office, objects, liability, capital, subscription (Tables A–E). AoA: internal rules, entrenchment (Tables F–J). Ultra vires memorandum = void, unratifiable. Constructive notice vs indoor management (Turquand) and its exceptions.
remember: Central + State holdings are added for the 51% Government-company test.
Voting power of subsidiaries is added for the subsidiary test.
A private subsidiary of a public company is deemed public.
Section 8 companies: no dividend, licence, 14-day meeting notice, fine ₹10 lakh–₹1 crore.
traps: Don't say acts ultra vires the memorandum can be ratified by special resolution.
Don't forget that holding/subsidiary companies cannot be small companies.
Don't apply indoor management to forgery or to insiders.
Don't compute called-up capital on issued instead of subscribed shares.

quickref.v: Small company: ≤₹10 cr paid-up and ≤₹100 cr turnover; not holding, subsidiary, Section 8
Promoter; formation; incorporation; effect; MoA–AoA binding
Authorised, issued, subscribed, called-up, paid-up capital

viva.q: What are the main features of a company?
viva.model: A company is a separate legal entity distinct from its members, it has perpetual succession so it continues even if members die or change, its members usually have limited liability, it is an artificial legal person acting through directors, and it may have a common seal, which is now optional.

kw: separate legal entity|separate entity|separate legal person|distinct from its members|separate person|different from its members|legal person|separate from members|separate from its members
perpetual|continues|continuity|never dies|does not die|existence not affected|succession
limited liability|liability limited|liability is limited|limited to unpaid|unpaid amount

points.pt: Artificial person acting through directors / common seal

viva.q: What was decided in Salomon versus Salomon, and when will courts lift the corporate veil?
viva.model: Salomon versus Salomon held that a company is a separate person from its members, so even a shareholder holding almost all the shares is not liable for its debts and can be its secured creditor. Courts lift the veil when the company is used for fraud or to evade a legal obligation, to evade tax, to find enemy character, or where a subsidiary is a mere agent of its parent.

points.pt: Salomon: company is a separate person from its members
Veil lifted for fraud / evading obligations
Other grounds: tax, enemy character, agency

viva.q: Define a private company under Section 2(68).
viva.model: A private company is one whose articles restrict the right to transfer its shares, limit the number of members to two hundred, excluding present and former employee-members and except an OPC, and prohibit any invitation to the public to subscribe for its securities.

viva.q: What is the doctrine of ultra vires and what is its effect?
viva.model: Ultra vires means beyond the powers. An act outside the objects in the memorandum is ultra vires the company and is void. It cannot be ratified even by all the shareholders, the company cannot sue or be sued on it, as held in Ashbury Railway Carriage versus Riche. An act beyond the directors' powers but within the company's powers can be ratified by members.

points.pt: Beyond the powers / objects in the memorandum

kw: cannot be ratified|no ratification|cannot ratify|never be ratified|not even unanimous|even unanimous|even all the shareholders|even by all

viva.q: Explain the doctrine of indoor management and its exceptions.
viva.model: Under the rule in Royal British Bank versus Turquand, an outsider dealing with a company may assume that internal formalities required by the articles have been complied with; he need not look into the internal proceedings. The exceptions are where he knew of the irregularity, where the circumstances were suspicious and he should have inquired, and forgery.

points.pt: Outsider may assume internal formalities complied with
kw: assume|presume|entitled to believe|need not inquire|need not check|not bound to inquire|need not look

viva.q: When is a company a subsidiary of another, and what is a Government company?
viva.model: Under Section 2(87) a company is a subsidiary of another if that other company controls the composition of its board of directors or controls more than one half of its total voting power, alone or together with its subsidiaries. Under Section 2(45) a Government company is one where the Central Government, one or more State Governments, or both together own fifty one percent or more of the paid-up capital, and it includes a subsidiary of such a company.

points.pt: Controls more than half of total voting power
kw: more than half|more than one half|more than 50|majority of voting|over 50|above 50|exceed 50|51|more than fifty

points.pt: Government company: at least 51% held by Central/State Governments

cases.title: The Orion group
cases.case: Orion Power Ltd is a public company in which the Central Government holds 35% and the State of Gujarat holds 20% of the paid-up share capital. Orion holds 60% of the voting power of Nova Solar Pvt Ltd and 22% of Zen Cables Ltd. Nova Solar's articles describe it as a private company; its paid-up capital is ₹5 crore and its turnover last year was ₹60 crore. Zen Cables has paid-up capital of ₹3 crore and a turnover of ₹40 crore.

mcqs.q: Is Orion Power Ltd a Government company?
options: Yes — Central and State holdings together are 55%
No — the Central Government holds less than 51%
No — only listed companies can be Government companies
Yes, but only for tax purposes
mcqs.explain: Section 2(45) counts Central and State holdings together: 35% + 20% = 55% ≥ 51%.

mcqs.q: What is the status of Nova Solar Pvt Ltd?
options: A Government company and deemed public company, being a subsidiary of Orion
mcqs.explain: More than half of its voting power is with Orion, making it a subsidiary. A subsidiary of a Government company is itself a Government company, and a subsidiary of a public company is deemed public (Section 2(71)).

mcqs.q: Can Nova Solar claim to be a small company?
options: No — a subsidiary company is excluded from Section 2(85)
Yes — its capital and turnover are within the limits
No — its turnover exceeds the limit
mcqs.explain: Holding and subsidiary companies are excluded even if within the money limits.

mcqs.q: Zen Cables Ltd is, in relation to Orion:
options: An associate company — at least 20% voting power
mcqs.explain: Section 2(6): significant influence = at least 20% of total voting power, without being a subsidiary.

cases.title: Lotus Ltd: powers, paperwork and a forgery
cases.case: Lotus Ltd's objects clause covers manufacture of ceramic tiles. Its articles allow the Board to borrow up to ₹5 crore and above that only with an ordinary resolution of members. (i) The Board borrowed ₹7 crore from a bank for expanding the tile plant without the members' resolution. (ii) The managing director signed a contract to buy a cricket franchise; members later ratified it unanimously. (iii) An employee obtained a loan from a finance company by producing a share certificate of Lotus bearing forged signatures of directors.

mcqs.q: Can the bank enforce the ₹7 crore loan against Lotus Ltd?
options: Yes — under the doctrine of indoor management it may assume the internal resolution was passed
No — the bank had constructive notice that a resolution was missing
No — borrowing is ultra vires the company
mcqs.explain: Ordinary resolutions are internal matters; the bank, an outsider, may presume regularity (Royal British Bank v. Turquand).

mcqs.q: What is the status of the cricket franchise contract?
options: Void — ultra vires the memorandum, and ratification cannot cure it
Valid because members ratified it unanimously
Voidable at the option of the company
Valid if the articles are altered
mcqs.explain: Ashbury Railway Carriage Co. v. Riche — an act beyond the objects is void and cannot be ratified.

mcqs.q: Can the finance company rely on the share certificate?
options: No — forgery is outside the doctrine of indoor management
Yes — internal matters need not be checked
Yes, because the seal was affixed
Only if it had inspected the memorandum
mcqs.explain: Ruben v. Great Fingall Consolidated — a forged document is a nullity.
